title: Fluctuation theorems and exact multi-allele fixation probabilities
authors: Emil A. Yuzbashyan, Alexander Feigel, Alexandre V. Morozov
abstract: A mutant gene that appears in a finite population will, in the long run, either disappear from it or become fixed, so that all members of the population will carry a copy of the mutant gene. Determining the fixation probability of a mutant gene is thus a prerequisite for modeling evolutionary dynamics in finite populations. Within the diffusion theory framework, the mutant's competition with the wild-type genes is described by the closed-form solution of a one-dimensional backward Kolmogorov equation for the mutant fixation probability, derived by Motoo Kimura in 1962. However, in asexual populations the rate of adaptation and the relative importance of alternative evolutionary pathways are shaped by clonal interference - the competition between several lineages arising from distinct beneficial or deleterious mutations. Quantitative descriptions of clonal interference require computing fixation probabilities in populations where multiple alleles are present simultaneously - a formidable mathematical problem which amounts to solving a multi-dimensional backward Kolmogorov equation. Here, we employ fluctuation theorems (a set of exact equalities in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics) in order to re-derive Kimura's fixation probability formula. When extended to multi-allele systems, fluctuation theorems provide a constraint which must be satisfied by any valid set of fixation probabilities. Moreover, we present a recursive analytical solution of the multi-allele fixation probability problem. We use our formalism to study the fate of a novel beneficial mutation in a clonal interference scenario, discovering substantial deviations between our exact treatment and the mean-field approximation in which the target mutation competes with a single effective genotype. Our formalism can be used to replace both explicit simulations and approximate analytical results in models of asexual evolution.
summary: This work develops an exact, analytical framework for calculating the fixation probability of beneficial mutations in populations with multiple competing alleles. By employing fluctuation theorems, the authors solve the multi-dimensional fixation probability problem, providing a rigorous alternative to standard mean-field approximations used in evolutionary modeling.
main_problem: The paper addresses the complex mathematical problem of determining the fixation probability of a mutant gene in finite populations, especially when multiple competing alleles are present (clonal interference).
main_result: The authors derive a recursive analytical solution for the multi-allele fixation probability problem using fluctuation theorems, showing substantial deviations from mean-field approximations in clonal interference scenarios.
method: The methodology combines the use of fluctuation theorems (exact equalities from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics) with solving multi-dimensional backward Kolmogorov equations, validated against stochastic simulations.
model_or_system: The model is population genetics, tracking genotype frequencies $x_i$ on a simplex $\Sigma^{M-1}$. Dynamics are governed by selection, mutation, and genetic drift, described by Fokker-Planck or Langevin equations.
key_observables: Fixation probabilities ($P_{fix}$), relative errors ($\varepsilon$), and the equilibrium distribution $P_{eq}(x)$.
important_parameters: Population size ($N$), number of alleles ($M$), selection coefficients ($s_i$), and mutation rates ($\mu$).
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on the framework of fluctuation theorems and involves comparing exact solutions against mean-field approximations and numerical simulations.
figures_summary: Figures compare series expansion results against Langevin and Wright-Fisher simulations for various numbers of alleles and selection coefficient regimes, demonstrating quantitative agreement.
paper_structure: The paper builds from re-deriving Kimura's formula using fluctuation theorems, extending this to a multi-allele framework, deriving a recursive analytical solution, and finally applying it to study clonal interference and comparing results against numerical benchmarks.
why_interesting: While focused on biology, the mathematical machinery—using fluctuation theorems to constrain solutions to complex stochastic differential equations (Fokker-Planck/Langevin)—is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics problems in AMO physics and open quantum systems.
